prompt: Which of these functions does `go test` run as a test?
hint: A name, a capital letter after it, and one parameter.

choices.text: `func testCount(t *testing.T)` in `wordcount_test.go`
choices.why: The name has to start with `Test`, capital T. A lower-case `test` is an ordinary unexported function.

choices.text: `func TestCount(t *testing.T)` in `wordcount_test.go`
choices.why: Right: the `Test` prefix, a capital after it, one `*testing.T`, in a `_test.go` file.

choices.text: `func TestCount()` in `wordcount_test.go`
choices.why: Without the `*testing.T` parameter there is no way to report a failure, and the go command refuses the signature.

choices.text: `func TestCount(t *testing.T)` in `wordcount.go`
choices.why: The function is right but the file is not: tests are compiled from files ending in `_test.go`.

prompt: The first `TestCount` failed on `fun` and `fast` but passed on `go`. What did that pattern tell the reader?
hint: What did `fun` and `fast` have in the sentence that `go` did not?

choices.text: That `Count` lost words at the end of the text
choices.why: `simple.` is the last word and was not checked; `fun.` sits in the middle and failed. Position was not the pattern.

choices.text: That lower-casing was broken
choices.why: `Go` and `go` were counted together as `go`, three times, so lower-casing worked.

choices.text: That punctuation stayed attached to the word
choices.why: Right. `fun.` and `fast,` carried a full stop and a comma; no `go` in the sentence touched one.

choices.text: That the scanner splits words on every letter that is not ASCII
choices.why: The sentence is all ASCII. `ScanWords` splits on spaces, which is why the punctuation stayed.

prompt: Why does the first test use `t.Fatalf` when `Count` returns an error, but `t.Errorf` for each count?
hint: Which checks are still worth making after each kind of failure?

choices.text: After an error the map is not worth checking; the counts are independent of each other
choices.why: Right. Stop where carrying on would only bury the real failure, carry on where each check says something new.

choices.text: `t.Fatalf` is for errors and `t.Errorf` is for wrong values
choices.why: Both take any message. The difference is whether the test function stops.

choices.text: `t.Errorf` does not mark the test as failed
choices.why: It does. Both mark the test failed; only `Fatalf` also stops it.

choices.text: `t.Fatalf` ends the whole `go test` run
choices.why: It ends the current test function (or subtest), and the other tests still run.

prompt: A test file's name has to end in ___ for `go test` to compile it and `go build` to leave it out.
A colleague's test fails, and they change the expected count in the test until it passes. When is that the right fix?

choices.text: Whenever the code was written before the test
choices.why: Order of writing says nothing about which one is right. `Count` existed first and was wrong about `fun.`.

choices.text: When the test asked for something the package should not do
choices.why: Right. `go's` was a decision about what a word is; `fun.` was a defect, and the code changed.

choices.text: When the failure is reported with `t.Errorf` rather than `t.Fatalf`
choices.why: Which method reported it says how the test carries on, not who was wrong.

choices.text: Never; a test is a specification
choices.why: A test can ask the wrong question, as `possessive` did. Deciding is part of the work.

prompt: What is the full name of the subtest started by `t.Run("accents", …)` inside `TestCount`?
hint: The `-v` output prints it after `=== RUN`.

choices.text: `accents`
choices.why: That is the string given to `t.Run`. The report adds the parent's name in front.

choices.text: `TestCount.accents`
choices.why: The separator is a slash, which is also what `-run` splits on.

choices.text: `TestCount/accents`
choices.why: Right: parent, slash, subtest.

choices.text: `TestCount_accents_3`
choices.why: Subtests are named by their string, not numbered by position.

prompt: In the run with five subtests, `possessive` failed. What happened to `empty`, the subtest after it?

choices.text: It was skipped, because the parent had already failed
choices.why: The parent fails only when the run is over; its other children still run.

choices.text: It ran and passed
choices.why: Right. A failure, even a `t.Fatalf`, ends the subtest that reported it and nothing else.

choices.text: It failed too, because subtests share one `*testing.T`
choices.why: Each subtest receives its own `t`, which is exactly what isolates the failures.

choices.text: It ran first, since `go test` reorders failing subtests to the end
choices.why: Subtests run in the order `t.Run` is called; the `-v` output lists them in source order.

prompt: You want to run only the `case` subtest of `TestCount`, and not a `lowercase` subtest that may be added one day. Which `-run` pattern does that?
hint: Each part of the pattern is a regular expression matched anywhere in that level of the name.

choices.text: `-run 'TestCount/case'`
choices.why: `case` matches inside `lowercase` too, since the expression is not anchored.

choices.text: `-run 'case'`
choices.why: With no slash this is matched against top-level test names, and no test is called `case`.

choices.text: `-run 'TestCount/^case$'`
choices.why: Right. The anchors make the second level match the whole name `case` and nothing longer.

choices.text: `-run 'TestCount' -v case`
choices.why: `-v` takes no argument; the extra word is a package path that does not exist.

prompt: Why did the course change the `possessive` test instead of making `Count` split `Go's` into `go`?

choices.text: Because the race detector reported a race in `TrimFunc`
choices.why: Nothing in this package is concurrent, and no race was involved.

choices.text: Because `unicode.IsLetter` cannot recognise an apostrophe
choices.why: It recognises it fine, as not a letter. The point is that `TrimFunc` only trims the ends.

choices.text: Splitting at apostrophes would break `don't` and `it's`
choices.why: Right. It was a decision about what a word is, and the test now records it.

choices.text: Because a failing test cannot be fixed by changing the code
choices.why: The first test was fixed by changing the code, in section 02.

prompt: Put the lines `go test -v` printed for the five subtests in the order they appear, starting with the first line.
hint: Every RUN line comes before the summary that closes the parent.

prompt: Without `t.Helper()`, the failing `wantCount` call reported line 7 of `demo_test.go`. What was on line 7?
hint: Which line does every call of the helper share?

choices.text: The second call, the one that asked about `fun`
choices.why: That was line 15, and it is what the report names once `t.Helper()` is added.

choices.text: The `t.Errorf` inside the helper
choices.why: Right, and every call goes through it, so the line says nothing about which call failed.

choices.text: The declaration `func TestDemo(t *testing.T)`
choices.why: A failure is reported at the line that recorded it, not at the test's declaration.

choices.text: The `import "testing"` line
choices.why: Line 3 is the import. Line 7 is inside `wantCount`.

prompt: `TestCountFile` writes `note.txt` into `t.TempDir()`. What happens to that directory if the test fails half way?

choices.text: It stays in `/tmp` so the failure can be examined
choices.why: It does not: the cleanup runs on failure as well. To keep a file for examination, copy it out with `t.Logf` pointing at it.

choices.text: It is removed only by `go clean -testcache`
choices.why: The test cache stores results, not temporary directories.

choices.text: It is reused by the next run of the same test
choices.why: Each call returns a new, empty directory; the run in the lesson had a fresh random number in its name.

choices.text: It is removed when the test ends, pass or fail
choices.why: Right. That is the point of `t.TempDir`: no litter after a failure, no collision between runs.

prompt: Which of these does a function registered with `t.Cleanup` suit? Choose all that apply.
hint: It runs after the test and its subtests finish.

choices.text: Stopping a server the test started
choices.why: Yes. The section names it.

choices.text: Putting back a package variable the test changed
choices.why: Yes, and `t.Setenv` does exactly this for an environment variable.

choices.text: Retrying the test if it failed
choices.why: A cleanup runs after the verdict and cannot change it.

choices.text: Running before the test, to prepare its input
choices.why: Preparation is ordinary code at the top of the test. A cleanup runs at the end.

prompt: Why does `TestCountFile` also check that a missing file gives an error matching `fs.ErrNotExist`?
hint: What may a caller of `CountFile` do with the error?

choices.text: Because `go test` counts a test with one check as incomplete
choices.why: The go command has no opinion on how many checks a test makes.

choices.text: Callers use `errors.Is` on it, and a careless wrap would break them
choices.why: Right. The test pins down a promise the function makes to its callers.

choices.text: To make sure `t.TempDir` was really emptied
choices.why: The directory is new and empty when the test starts; `missing.txt` was never written.

choices.text: Because `os.Open` panics on a missing file
choices.why: It returns an error, which is what the test examines.

prompt: Match each method of `*testing.T` with what it does.
hint: Five methods from the section, four of them here.

pairs.right: report the caller's line, not this one
a new empty directory, removed at the end
set a variable for this test and restore it
cancelled just before the cleanups run

right_distractors: run the test again with the race detector

hint: Count the indented PASS lines under `TestCount`.

prompt: A test checks that `Count` gives `"the": 2` for a paragraph, and passes. A month later somebody changes `notLetter` so digits are trimmed too. Which subtest in this lesson's final test file would catch that change?
hint: Look for a case whose words contain digits.

choices.text: `punctuation`
choices.why: Its sentence has no digit in it, so trimming digits changes nothing there.

choices.text: `accents`
choices.why: Accented letters are letters; trimming digits leaves them alone.

choices.text: None of them: no case has a word with a digit
choices.why: Right. A behaviour no test exercises can change silently, which is lesson 30's subject.

choices.text: `empty`
choices.why: An empty text has no words to trim.
